newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO sets fresh China entry talks for March.
newsitem.headline: WTO sets fresh China entry talks for March.

text.p: China and its trading partners will resume negotiations on March 6 on its bid to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), a WTO spokesman said on Thursday.
The talks, the first round to be held this year, follow new signals from China of a willingness to drop many of its biggest trade barriers in order to enter the 130-member trade watchdog.

China applied in 1987 to join the WTO's predecessor body, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). But accession has been stalled due to demands by the United States and other trading powers for Beijing to phase out government controls.
"A formal meeting of the WTO working party is scheduled for March 6," a WTO spokesman told Reuters.
Bilateral sessions with the Chinese delegation are expected to be held earlier in the week, according to trade sources.
In Washington on Wednesday, Secretary of Commerce William Daley said he was encouraged by China indicating a willingess to drop many of its biggest trade barriers to win WTO membership.
"As (U.S. Trade Representative Charlene) Barshefsky said, though, what's written is more important than what's said, so we will wait to see the written word," Daley told reporters.

The WTO working party negotiating the terms of China's accession protocol last met in November. Since then, Chinese officials have held bilateral trade talks with the United States, European Union and Japan on its stalled bid to join WTO.
The U.S. official said the U.S. trade delegation expected to see Beijing's latest offer in writing during talks in Geneva the first week in March.
A Chinese foreign trade official, speaking in Beijing on Wednesday, said his country hoped to make new progress on its WTO application.
"But China's entry will hinge on WTO members. We have already presented what we can offer to members and it is up to them to decide," he said.
Last April, China slashed its average import tariff to 23 percent from 35 percent, the biggest single cut the country has implemented. Beijing says it plans more reductions.
